questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A vertical tube is completely filled with water. A small sound source of constant frequency is held slightly above the open upper end. Water runs out from the lower end and a number of resonance positions are detected. The first of these occurs when the water surface is 15 cm below the top of the tube and the next occurs at 49 cm. The speed of sound in air as 330 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$.

What is the frequency of the source?
questions.stemText: A vertical tube is completely filled with water. A small sound source of constant frequency is held slightly above the open upper end. Water runs out from the lower end and a number of resonance positions are detected. The first of these occurs when the water surface is 15 cm below the top of the tube and the next occurs at 49 cm. The speed of sound in air as 330 m s−1. What is the frequency of the source? A 390 Hz B 490 Hz C 500 Hz D 550 Hz

appearances.originalFile: grail:9605 ACJC 2022 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must infer the wavelength from the spacing of successive resonances.
questions.misconception: Ignoring the open-end correction

explanation.body: Consecutive resonant lengths differ by half a wavelength, so $\lambda/2=0.49-0.15=0.34\ \mathrm{m}$ and $\lambda=0.68\ \mathrm{m}$. Using $v=f\lambda$ gives $330=f(0.68)$ and hence $f=490\ \mathrm{Hz}$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Implies an 85 cm wavelength, larger than twice the measured resonance spacing.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Rounds the calculated frequency too coarsely.
perOption.D: Treats the first 15 cm length as exactly one quarter wavelength.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
In a Young’s double slit experiment, a red light from a laser is incident on the source slit $\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{o}}$ and passes through the double slits $\mathrm{S}_{1}$ and $\mathrm{S}_{2}$, producing red bright fringes as shown the figure below.

Subsequently, a transparent thin glass block is placed in front of $\mathrm{S}_{1}$.

Which observation is correct?
questions.stemText: In a Young’s double slit experiment, a red light from a laser is incident on the source slit So and passes through the double slits S1 and S2, producing red bright fringes as shown the figure below. Subsequently, a transparent thin glass block is placed in front of S1. S1 red light source (laser) central line So S2 Which observation is correct? A The fringe separation will decrease. B The fringe separation will be non-uniform. C The contrast between bright and dark fringes will increase. D The central maximum will be shifted upwards.

options.label: B
options.text: The fringe separation will be non-uniform.

options.label: C
options.text: The contrast between bright and dark fringes will increase.

options.label: D
options.text: The central maximum will be shifted upwards.

appearances.originalFile: grail:9605 ACJC 2022 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must connect the added phase delay to the direction of the fringe shift.
questions.misconception: Confusing fringe shift with fringe spacing

explanation.body: Glass has a higher refractive index than air, so the light travels more slowly and has a shorter wavelength inside the glass. The block therefore contains more wavelengths than the same thickness of air. The central maximum shifts upwards, where the shorter geometric path from $S_1$ compensates for the extra phase delay.

perOption.A: Uses the wavelength in glass to predict the fringe spacing on the screen.
perOption.B: Treats the delay from the thin glass block as varying from fringe to fringe.
perOption.C: Confuses the phase delay with an improvement in the balance of the two beam intensities.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A narrow beam of monochromatic light falls on a diffraction grating at normal incidence. The second order diffracted beam occurs at an angle of $31^\circ$ to the normal.

What is the total number of intensity maxima from the grating that can be observed?

A 3
B 4
C 7
D 9

stemImage.alt: Question 18: A narrow beam of monochromatic light falls on a diffraction grating at normal incidence. The second order diffracted beam occurs at an angle of 31 to the norma

appearances.originalFile: grail:10416 ACJC 2023 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The grating equation gives the order limit, which must be converted into a count on both sides.
questions.misconception: Rounding the maximum order up

explanation.body: For the second order, $d\sin31^\circ=2\lambda$. Since $\sin\theta\leq 1$, the order satisfies $m\leq d/\lambda=2/\sin31^\circ\approx3.88$. The allowed orders are $0,\pm1,\pm2,\pm3$, giving seven maxima.

perOption.A: Counts only the three nonzero orders on one side.
perOption.B: Counts the central maximum and the orders on just one side.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Rounds the order limit up and counts a fourth-order maximum on each side.

The distance between the two consecutive positions when the sound is at maximum loudness is $x$.

What is the wavelength of the sound emitted by the tuning fork?

A $x/2$
B $x$
C $3x/2$
D $2x$

questions.difficultyReason: The student must recognize what the change in air-column length measures.
questions.misconception: Confusing resonance spacing with a full wavelength

explanation.body: The air column has a displacement node at the water surface and an antinode near the open end. Successive resonances occur at effective lengths that differ by $\lambda/2$, so $x=\lambda/2$ and $\lambda=2x$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The angular resolution of a vertical slit for a pair of objects is $4.0\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{rad}$.

What is the new angular resolution if the width of the slit is doubled?

A $1.0\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{rad}$
B $2.0\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{rad}$
C $8.0\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{rad}$
D $16\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{rad}$

stemImage.alt: Question 19: The angular resolution of a vertical slit for a pair of objects is 4.0  10─2 rad. What is the new angular resolution if the width of the slit is doubled?

appearances.originalFile: grail:14529 (ACJC) 2024 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The Rayleigh criterion gives an immediate inverse-proportion calculation.
questions.misconception: Assuming angular resolution increases with slit width

explanation.body: By Rayleigh’s criterion, $\theta\approx\lambda/b$. Doubling the slit width gives $\theta_{\mathrm{new}}/\theta_{\mathrm{old}}=b_{\mathrm{old}}/b_{\mathrm{new}}=0.5$. The new angular resolution is $2.0\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{rad}$.

perOption.A: Assumes inverse-square dependence on slit width.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Assumes direct rather than inverse proportionality.
perOption.D: Assumes angular resolution grows as the square of slit width.

Which graph shows the variation of $x$ with $\lambda$?

[All four graphs plot $x$ against $\lambda/\mathrm{nm}$ from 400 to 700, with $x=0$ at the horizontal axis.
A: Straight line rising from $x=0$ at 400 nm.
B: Straight line rising from a positive $x$ at 400 nm.
C: Straight line falling with wavelength and remaining above zero.
D: Curve falling steeply at first and flattening close to zero.]

appearances.originalFile: grail:19926 ACJC 2025 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The main challenge is reading the truncated wavelength axis.
questions.misconception: Treating 400 nm as the origin

explanation.body: The double-slit relation is $\lambda=ax/D$, so $x=\lambda D/a$. Fringe separation is directly proportional to wavelength, and the plotted range starts at $400\ \mathrm{nm}$, where the separation is already positive.

perOption.A: Treats the left edge of the graph as zero wavelength.
perOption.B: Correct. The spacing rises linearly from a positive value at 400 nm.
perOption.C: Makes the spacing decrease linearly as wavelength increases.
perOption.D: Makes the spacing decrease nonlinearly as wavelength increases.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The diameter of the receiving dish of a telescope is $5.1\ \mathrm{m}$. It receives light of wavelength $0.40\ \mu\mathrm{m}$ from two point sources at a distance of $2.8\times10^{25}\ \mathrm{m}$ away.

What is the minimum separation of the two points sources so that the light from them can be resolved?

A. $1.1\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{m}$
B. $2.2\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{m}$
C. $1.8\times10^{32}\ \mathrm{m}$
D. $3.6\times10^{32}\ \mathrm{m}$

stemImage.alt: Question 17: The diameter of the receiving dish of a telescope is 5.1 m. It receives light of wavelength  25 2.8 10 m 0.40 μm from two point sources at a distance of away.

appearances.originalFile: grail:19926 ACJC 2025 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1
DHS Physics Prelim 2026/H2/DHS 2026 Y6 Physics H2 P1 Prelim (for external sharing).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The calculation links angular resolution to linear separation using the small-angle approximation.
questions.misconception: Inverting the diffraction angle

explanation.body: The limiting angle is $\theta\approx\lambda/b$, where $b$ is the dish diameter. By the small-angle approximation, $x/D\approx\theta$, so $x=\lambda D/b=(0.40\times10^{-6})(2.8\times10^{25})/5.1=2.2\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Halves the full source separation found from the limiting angle.
perOption.B: Correct. The minimum separation is the distance multiplied by the limiting angle.
perOption.C: Inverting the limiting angle and then halving the resulting distance gives this value.
perOption.D: Divides the source distance by the limiting angle instead of multiplying.

questions.stem:
A transmitter produces microwaves that travel in air towards a metal plate as shown.

The microwaves have a wavelength of 12.0 cm.

A microwave receiver is initially placed at position X where it detects an intensity maximum. The receiver is then slowly moved away from X directly towards the plate.

What is the number of intensity minima that are detected by the receiver as it moves from X to a position that is 33.5 cm away from X?
questions.stemText: A transmitter produces microwaves that travel in air towards a metal plate as shown. The microwaves have a wavelength of 12.0 cm. A microwave receiver is initially placed at position X where it detects an intensity maximum. The receiver is then slowly moved away from X directly towards the plate. What is the number of intensity minima that are detected by the receiver as it moves from X to a position that is 33.5 cm away from X? A 2 B 3 C 5 D 6

appearances.originalFile: grail:19926 ACJC 2025 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Students must locate the first node from an antinode before counting the remaining nodes.
questions.misconception: Counting nodes from the wrong starting phase

explanation.body: The receiver travels $33.5/12.0=2.79$ wavelengths. Since X is an antinode, the nodes occur $0.25\lambda$, $0.75\lambda$, $1.25\lambda$, $1.75\lambda$, $2.25\lambda$ and $2.75\lambda$ from X, so six minima are detected.

perOption.A: Counts only complete wavelengths, missing the nodes spaced half a wavelength apart.
perOption.B: Counting just the nodes at quarter-wavelength plus whole-wavelength offsets skips every second node.
perOption.C: Counting only complete half-wavelength intervals misses the sixth node at $2.75\lambda$.
perOption.D: Correct. Six nodes lie within the distance travelled.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Monochromatic light is incident normally on a single slit. The resulting diffraction pattern is observed on a screen. The width of the central maximum of the diffraction pattern is x.

The distance between the single slit and the screen is much greater than the slit width and is unchanged.

The light source is replaced by another light source of light with twice the wavelength, and the single slit is replaced by one that has half the slit width.

What is the linear width of the new central maximum in terms of x?
questions.stemText: Monochromatic light is incident normally on a single slit. The resulting diffraction pattern is observed on a screen. The width of the central maximum of the diffraction pattern is x. The distance between the single slit and the screen is much greater than the slit width and is unchanged. The light source is replaced by another light source of light with twice the wavelength, and the single slit is replaced by one that has half the slit width. What is the linear width of the new central maximum in terms of x? A 0.5x B x C 2x D 4x

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Small-angle single-slit relation with two simultaneous factor changes.
questions.misconception: Thinking the two changes cancel

explanation.body:
$\sin\theta = \dfrac{\lambda}{b}$. Since the slit-screen distance $D$ is much greater than the slit width, the angle is small.

$\theta = \dfrac{\tfrac{1}{2}x}{D} = \dfrac{\lambda}{b}$, so $x = \dfrac{2\lambda D}{b}$.

New width: $x' = \dfrac{2(2\lambda)D}{b/2} = \dfrac{8\lambda D}{b} = 4x$.

perOption.A: Wrong proportionality; $x \propto \lambda/b$, so both changes widen the pattern.
perOption.B: Assumes the two changes cancel, but doubling λ and halving b both increase the width.
perOption.C: Accounts for only one of the two changes.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Monochromatic light is incident normally on a diffraction grating. First and second order images are observed at angles of diffraction $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ respectively. [Diagram: monochromatic light incident normally on a vertical grating; diffracted beams to a screen labelled n = 0, n = 1 and n = 2 on each side, with $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ measured from the central n = 0 direction.] What is the relation between the angles of diffraction and between the intensities of light in the two orders? (angles of diffraction; intensities) A $\theta_2 = 2\theta_1$; same B $\theta_2 = 2\theta_1$; second order dimmer C $\theta_2 > 2\theta_1$; same D $\theta_2 > 2\theta_1$; second order dimmer

stemImage.alt: Question 15: Monochromatic light is incident normally on a diffraction grating. First and second order images are observed at angles of diffraction 1 and 2 respectively. d

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires recognising that sin θ, not θ, scales with order, and recalling that higher orders are dimmer.
questions.misconception: Assuming $\theta \propto n$ rather than $\sin\theta \propto n$

explanation.body:
$\sin\theta_1 = \dfrac{(1)\lambda}{d}$ and $\sin\theta_2 = \dfrac{(2)\lambda}{d}$, so $\sin\theta_2 = 2\sin\theta_1$.

The rate of increase of $\sin\theta$ decreases as $\theta$ increases from 0 to 90°, so $\theta_2 > 2\theta_1$.

At higher orders, since the distance travelled by the light increases, intensity decreases, so the second order is dimmer.

perOption.A: Assumes $\theta \propto n$, but it is $\sin\theta$ that is proportional to $n$; also intensity is not the same.
perOption.B: Assumes $\theta \propto n$; it is $\sin\theta$ that doubles.
perOption.C: Angle relation is right, but higher orders are dimmer.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.stemText: The lens of a spy satellite orbiting at 200 km has a diameter of 35 cm. What is the shortest distance this camera can resolve on the surface of the Earth if a wavelength of 500 nm is used? A $2.9\times10^{-4}$ m B 0.14 m C 0.29 m D 2.9 m

stemImage.alt: Question 16: The lens of a spy satellite orbiting at 200 km has a diameter of 35 cm. What is the shortest distance this camera can resolve on the surface of the Earth if a w

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Rayleigh criterion plus small-angle geometry with unit conversions.
questions.misconception: Unit/power-of-ten errors with km and nm

explanation.body:
Using the Rayleigh criterion, $\theta = \dfrac{\lambda}{b} = \dfrac{x}{D}$.

$x = \dfrac{\lambda D}{b} = \dfrac{(500\times10^{-9})(200\times10^{3})}{35\times10^{-2}} = 0.29\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Uses 200 m instead of 200 km for the orbital height.
perOption.B: Introduces an extra factor of $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses a lens diameter of 3.5 cm instead of 35 cm.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
In a double-slit interference experiment, one slit transmits waves of twice the amplitude compared to the other slit. The intensity at one of the bright fringes on the screen is $I_o$.

What is the intensity at the dark fringe closest to this bright fringe?

A zero
B $I_o/2$
C $I_o/4$
D $I_o/9$

stemImage.alt: Question 17: In a double-slit interference experiment, one slit transmits waves of twice the amplitude compared to the other slit. The intensity at one of the bright fringes

appearances.originalFile: grail:9611 ASRJC 2022 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must combine unequal amplitudes before squaring their ratio.
questions.misconception: Assuming all destructive interference gives zero intensity

explanation.body: Intensity is proportional to amplitude squared. The bright fringe has $I_o\propto(2A+A)^2$ and the dark fringe has $I\propto(2A-A)^2$. Thus $I/I_o=(A/3A)^2=1/9$.

perOption.A: Complete cancellation requires equal amplitudes.
perOption.B: The factor of two compares the individual slit amplitudes and gives no fringe intensity ratio.
perOption.C: This squares the ratio of the individual slit amplitudes in place of the resultant amplitudes.
perOption.D: Correct. The dark-fringe intensity is one ninth of the bright-fringe intensity.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A space station orbits at a height of 335 km above the surface of the Earth. It carries two panels separated by a distance of 25 m. The panels reflect light of wavelength 500 nm towards an observer on the Earth’s surface.

The observer views the panels with a telescope that has an aperture diameter of 200 mm. Assume that the panels act as point sources of light for the observer.

Which of the following is correct?

Will the two images seen by the observer be resolved? | Angular separation of two panels as measured from aperture / rad
A Yes | $2.5\times10^{-6}$
B Yes | $7.5\times10^{-5}$
C No | $2.5\times10^{-6}$
D No | $7.5\times10^{-5}$

stemImage.alt: Question 18: A space station orbits at a height of 335 km above the surface of the Earth. It carries two panels separated by a distance of 25 m. The panels reflect light of

appearances.originalFile: grail:9611 ASRJC 2022 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must calculate the observed angle and compare it with the diffraction limit.
questions.misconception: Confusing angular separation with the resolution limit

explanation.body: Using $s=r\theta$, the angular separation is $\theta=25/(335\times10^3)=7.46\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{rad}$, or $7.5\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{rad}$. The minimum angle of resolution is $\theta_m\approx\lambda/b=(500\times10^{-9})/(200\times10^{-3})=2.5\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{rad}$. The images are resolved because the angular separation exceeds this minimum.

perOption.A: The angle quoted is the resolution limit.
perOption.B: Correct. The panel separation exceeds the resolution limit.
perOption.C: This substitutes the resolution limit for the larger actual separation.
perOption.D: The quoted separation exceeds the minimum needed for resolution.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Monochromatic light is incident on a pair of narrow slits a distance of 0.1 mm apart. A series of bright and dark fringes are observed on a screen a distance of 2.0 m away. The distance between adjacent bright fringes is 8.0 mm.

What is the path difference between the light waves from the two slits that meet at the second order dark fringe?
questions.stemText: Monochromatic light is incident on a pair of narrow slits a distance of 0.1 mm apart. A series of bright and dark fringes are observed on a screen a distance of 2.0 m away. The distance between adjacent bright fringes is 8.0 mm. What is the path difference between the light waves from the two slits that meet at the second order dark fringe? A 2.0 × $10^{-7}$ m B 4.0 × $10^{-7}$ m C 6.0 × $10^{-7}$ m D 8.0 × $10^{-7}$ m

appearances.originalFile: grail:14523 ASRJC 2024 JC2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Requires finding the wavelength and identifying the second destructive-interference condition.
questions.misconception: Using a whole-wavelength path difference for a dark fringe.

explanation.body: From $x=\lambda D/a$, the wavelength is $\lambda=(0.008)(0.0001)/2.0=4.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$. The slit sources are in phase, so dark fringes occur at path differences $(n+\tfrac12)\lambda$ with $n=0,1,\dots$. The second dark fringe has $n=1$, so its path difference is $1.5\lambda=6.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Uses $\lambda/2$, which gives the first dark fringe.
perOption.B: Uses $\lambda$, which gives the first bright fringe away from the centre.
perOption.C: Correct. The second dark fringe has a path difference of one and a half wavelengths.
perOption.D: Uses $2\lambda$, which gives the second bright fringe away from the centre.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A musical instrument called a bugle is a long tube with a mouthpiece at one end. The other end is an open end and flared, as shown.

A musician maintains stationary sound waves with a node at the mouthpiece and an antinode at the other end. The lowest frequency of sound that the bugle can produce is 92 Hz.

Which different frequencies of sound can be produced by the bugle?
questions.stemText: A musical instrument called a bugle is a long tube with a mouthpiece at one end. The other end is an open end and flared, as shown. A musician maintains stationary sound waves with a node at the mouthpiece and an antinode at the other end. The lowest frequency of sound that the bugle can produce is 92 Hz. Which different frequencies of sound can be produced by the bugle? A 92 Hz, 138 Hz, 184 Hz, 230 Hz, 276 Hz B 92 Hz, 184 Hz, 276 Hz, 368 Hz, 460 Hz C 92 Hz, 276 Hz, 460 Hz, 644 Hz, 828 Hz D 92 Hz, 276 Hz, 828 Hz, 2484 Hz, 7452 Hz

appearances.originalFile: grail:14523 ASRJC 2024 JC2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Requires identifying the allowed harmonics for a tube with a node at one end and an antinode at the other.
questions.misconception: Treating a node–antinode tube as supporting every integer harmonic.

explanation.body: The node at the mouthpiece and the antinode at the open end allow only odd harmonics. Their frequencies follow $(2n+1)f$ for $n=0,1,2,\dots$, with $f=92\ \mathrm{Hz}$, giving $92$, $276$, $460$, $644$ and $828\ \mathrm{Hz}$ as the first five.

perOption.A: Includes frequencies such as 138 Hz that are not odd integer multiples of the fundamental.
perOption.B: Includes even harmonics such as 184 Hz.
perOption.C: Correct. These are the first five odd harmonics.
perOption.D: Successive tripling skips allowed harmonics such as 460 Hz.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Light of wavelength $\lambda$ is emitted from two point sources R and S and falls onto a distant screen.

[Point source R is above point source S on the left. Point P is marked on the vertical screen to their right. NOT TO SCALE.]

At point P on the screen, the light intensity is zero.

What could explain the zero intensity at P?

A Light from the two sources is emitted $180^\circ$ out of phase and the path difference to P is $\lambda$.
B Light from the two sources is emitted $180^\circ$ out of phase and the path difference to P is $\tfrac12\lambda$.
C Light from the two sources is emitted $90^\circ$ out of phase and the path difference to P is $\lambda$.
D Light from the two sources is emitted in phase and the path difference to P is $\lambda$.

stemImage.alt: Question 16: Light of wavelength  is emitted from two point sources R and S and falls onto a distant screen. At point P on the screen, the light intensity is zero. What cou

appearances.originalFile: grail:18733 ASRJC 2025 Prelim P1 H2 Physics QN paper

questions.difficultyReason: It requires combining the source phase difference with the phase difference caused by the paths.
questions.misconception: Ignoring the initial phase difference between the sources.

explanation.body: The phase difference at P is the source phase difference plus $2\pi$ times the path difference divided by the wavelength. Zero intensity requires destructive interference, for which the waves arrive with a phase difference of an odd multiple of $\pi$.

perOption.A: Correct. The phase difference is $2\pi+\pi=3\pi$.
perOption.B: The phase difference is $\tfrac12(2\pi)+\pi=2\pi$, giving constructive interference.
perOption.C: The phase difference is $2\pi+\tfrac{\pi}{2}=\tfrac{5\pi}{2}$, which does not give cancellation.
perOption.D: The phase difference is $2\pi+0=2\pi$, giving constructive interference.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A beam of red light of wavelength 720 nm is incident normally on a diffraction grating and produces a diffraction pattern on a screen placed parallel to the grating.

The beam of red light is replaced with a beam of electromagnetic radiation of wavelength X, which is incident normally on the same diffraction grating.

The third-order maximum for the electromagnetic radiation of wavelength X is at the same position on the screen as the second-order maximum for the red light.

What is wavelength X?
questions.stemText: A beam of red light of wavelength 720 nm is incident normally on a diffraction grating and produces a diffraction pattern on a screen placed parallel to the grating. The beam of red light is replaced with a beam of electromagnetic radiation of wavelength X, which is incident normally on the same diffraction grating. The third-order maximum for the electromagnetic radiation of wavelength X is at the same position on the screen as the second-order maximum for the red light. What is wavelength X? A 480 nm B 540 nm C 960 nm D 1100 nm

appearances.originalFile: grail:18733 ASRJC 2025 Prelim P1 H2 Physics QN paper

questions.difficultyReason: Matching the screen positions lets the student equate the order–wavelength products.
questions.misconception: Assuming wavelength increases with order at a fixed diffraction angle.

explanation.body: The grating equation is $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$. Both maxima have the same $d$ and $\theta$, so $3\lambda_X=2\lambda_{\mathrm{red}}=2(720\times10^{-9})\ \mathrm{m}$. Thus $\lambda_X=480\ \mathrm{nm}$.

perOption.A: Correct. Both orders have the same product of order and wavelength.
perOption.B: Uses a wavelength ratio of three quarters instead of two thirds.
perOption.C: Makes the third-order wavelength larger even though the order–wavelength product is fixed.
perOption.D: Reverses the order ratio, giving about $1100\ \mathrm{nm}$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: The two lowest frequencies at which an open narrow tube resonates are 256 Hz and 512 Hz. If one of the ends is closed, what are the two lowest frequencies at which it would now resonate?
questions.stemText: The two lowest frequencies at which an open narrow tube resonates are 256 Hz and 512 Hz. If one of the ends is closed, what are the two lowest frequencies at which it would now resonate? A 128 Hz and 256 Hz B 128 Hz and 384 Hz C 384 Hz and 640 Hz D 768 Hz and 1536 Hz

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs to find the fundamental of the open tube and convert to the closed-tube harmonic series.
questions.misconception: Assuming closed tubes support all harmonics, or that closing an end raises frequency

explanation.body: The open tube has fundamental wavelength $2L$, so $v=f_0\lambda_0=(256)(2L)=512L$. With one end closed the longest resonant wavelength is $4L$, giving $f_1=512L/(4L)=128\ \mathrm{Hz}$. The next wavelength is $4L/3$, giving $f_2=512L/(4L/3)=384\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

perOption.A: Includes the even harmonic at 256 Hz, which the tube with one closed end cannot support.
perOption.B: Correct. These are the fundamental and third harmonic.
perOption.C: Gives the third and fifth harmonics and skips the 128 Hz fundamental.
perOption.D: Both frequencies are even multiples of the new fundamental.

Monochromatic light of wavelength 520 nm is directed perpendicularly onto a diffraction grating. The second-order diffraction lines are observed at $56°$ to each other.

[Diagram: light of wavelength 520 nm falls normally on a diffraction grating; the two second-order beams diverge to a screen with an angle of $56°$ between them.]

What is the total number of diffraction lines produced by the grating?

A 4   B 5   C 8   D 9

stemImage.alt: Question 15: Monochromatic light of wavelength 520 nm is directed perpendicularly onto a diffraction grating. The second-order diffraction lines are observed at 56 to each

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must halve the angle, find $d/\lambda$ and then count the orders on both sides plus the central maximum.
questions.misconception: Using 56° rather than 28° as the diffraction angle, or forgetting the central maximum

explanation.body:
The second-order lines are $56°$ apart, so each is at $\theta = 28°$: $d\sin 28° = 2\lambda \Rightarrow \dfrac{d}{\lambda} = \dfrac{2}{\sin 28°}$.

From $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$ and $\sin\theta \le 1$: $n \le \dfrac{d}{\lambda} = \dfrac{2}{\sin 28°} = 4.26$, so $n_{\max} = 4$.

Number of diffraction lines $= (4 \times 2) + 1 = 9$

perOption.A: Gives only the highest order, $n_{\max}$, instead of counting lines on both sides and the central maximum.
perOption.B: Counts only one side of the central maximum, plus the zeroth order.
perOption.C: Counts both sides but leaves out the zeroth-order (central) line.
perOption.D: Correct. $n_{\max} = 4$ on each side, plus the central maximum.

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must choose a visible wavelength themselves and combine the Rayleigh criterion with the small-angle approximation.

explanation.body:
Distance $r = 20 \times 10^{16}\ \mathrm{m}$. By the Rayleigh criterion, $\theta \approx \lambda/D$, so the minimum separation is $s = r\theta = r\dfrac{\lambda}{D}$.

Violet (400 nm): $s = \dfrac{(20 \times 10^{16})(400 \times 10^{-9})}{3.0} = 2.7 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{m}$

Red (700 nm): $s = \dfrac{(20 \times 10^{16})(700 \times 10^{-9})}{3.0} = 4.7 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{m}$

Across the visible range, the order of magnitude is $10^{10}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.B: Correct. $s = r\lambda/D \approx 10^{10}\ \mathrm{m}$ for visible light.
perOption.C: Too large by a factor of about 100, likely from a powers-of-ten slip in $\lambda$ (for example, using micrometres as nanometres).
perOption.D: Far too large. It does not follow from $s = r\lambda/D$ with visible wavelengths.

The figure shows the top view of a human head with the two ears 22 cm apart. Sound waves of wavelength 1.7 m from a distant source reach the ears at an angle of $25^{\mathrm{o}}$ to the horizontal.

questions.difficultyReason: Requires working out the path difference from the geometry before applying $\Delta\phi = 2\pi\Delta x/\lambda$.
questions.misconception: Uses $\cos$ instead of $\sin$ for the path difference.

explanation.body:
Path difference between the ears $= 0.22\sin 25^\circ\ \mathrm{m}$.

$\Delta\phi = \dfrac{0.22\sin25^\circ}{1.7}\times 2\pi = 0.34\ \mathrm{rad}$

perOption.A: Correct. Path difference $0.22\sin25^\circ$ converted to phase.
perOption.B: Does not match the correct geometry; likely a slip in the angle or wavelength.
perOption.C: Uses $\cos25^\circ$ instead of $\sin25^\circ$ for the path difference.
perOption.D: Omits the angle, using the full $0.22\ \mathrm{m}$ as the path difference.

questions.stem:
A student observed two blue dots of 5 mm diameter on a screen. The distance between the two dots is 7.0 mm. The student who is facing the screen takes a few steps backwards and stops walking when the two dots are no longer resolved.

The student wishes to still resolve the two dots at this distance from the screen. What should she do?

The student who is facing the screen takes a few steps backwards and stops walking when the two dots are no longer resolved. The student wishes to still resolve the two dots at this distance from the screen. What should she do? A darken the room to increase the size of the pupil of the eye. B change the colour of the two dots from blue to red. C make the blue dots slightly brighter. D make the two dots closer.

options.label: A
options.text: darken the room to increase the size of the pupil of the eye.

options.label: B
options.text: change the colour of the two dots from blue to red.

options.label: C
options.text: make the blue dots slightly brighter.

appearances.originalFile: grail:10482 TJC 2023 H2 Prelim Paper 1

questions.difficultyReason: Direct application of the Rayleigh criterion in a qualitative setting.

explanation.body:
By Rayleigh's criterion, the minimum angle of resolution is $\theta \approx \lambda/b$, where the pupil size acts as the slit width $b$.

If $b$ increases, $\theta$ decreases, so the dots are easier to resolve. Darkening the room enlarges the pupil.

perOption.A: Correct. Larger pupil $b$ gives smaller $\lambda/b$, so closer dots can be resolved.
perOption.B: Red light has a longer wavelength, increasing $\lambda/b$ and making resolution worse.
perOption.C: Brightness does not change the minimum resolvable angle.
perOption.D: Moving the dots closer decreases their angular separation, making them harder to resolve.

questions.stem: A progressive wave of amplitude A has intensity I. This wave combines with another coherent wave of amplitude 0.6A at a point P in space. The 2 waves started out anti-phase and arrives at point P with a path difference of 4 wavelengths. What is the resultant intensity of the combined waves in terms of I at point P?
questions.stemText: A progressive wave of amplitude A has intensity I. This wave combines with another coherent wave of amplitude 0.6A at a point P in space. The 2 waves started out anti-phase and arrives at point P with a path difference of 4 wavelengths. What is the resultant intensity of the combined waves in terms of I at point P? A 0.16 I B 0.4I C 1.6I D 2.6I

appearances.originalFile: grail:14595 2024 TJC H2 Prelim Paper 1

questions.difficultyReason: Combines phase reasoning from initial antiphase and path difference with $I\propto A^2$.
questions.misconception: Ignoring the initial phase difference of $\pi$

explanation.body:
$I \propto A^2$, so $I = kA^2$.

The waves start in antiphase and have a path difference of a whole number of wavelengths, so they arrive in antiphase: resultant amplitude $= A - 0.6A = 0.4A$.

$I_R = k(0.4A)^2 = 0.16kA^2 = 0.16I$.

perOption.A: Correct. Destructive interference with amplitude $0.4A$.
perOption.B: Uses $0.4A$ but forgets to square it.
perOption.C: Treats the waves as in phase and adds intensities ($1+0.6$) without squaring.
perOption.D: Adds the amplitudes (constructive) and forgets to square: $1.6\ldots$ then adds.

The second order fringe appears on a screen 75 cm away from the diffraction grating and 20 cm away from the central fringe. 75 cm laser 20 cm diffraction grating screen What is the wavelength of the laser beam? questions.difficultyReason: Needs the angle from screen geometry, grating spacing from lines per mm, and the correct order.
questions.misconception: Using $\sin\theta = 20/75$ or the wrong order $n$

explanation.body:
$\tan\theta = \dfrac{20}{75}$, so $\theta = 14.9^\circ$.

Using $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$ with $d = 1/N$:

$\dfrac{10^{-3}}{300}\sin14.9^\circ = 2\lambda$

$\lambda = 429\ \mathrm{nm}$.

perOption.A: Correct. $\theta$ from the geometry, then $d\sin\theta=2\lambda$.
perOption.B: Uses $\sin\theta = 20/75$ instead of $\tan\theta$.
perOption.C: Uses $n=1$ instead of $n=2$ (gives double: 858 nm).
perOption.D: Uses $\sin\theta = 20/75$ and $n=1$.

questions.stemText:
Monochromatic light of wavelength $490\ \mathrm{nm}$ falls normally on a diffraction grating that has $6\times10^5$ lines per metre. Which one of the following is correct?

A The first order is observed at angle of diffraction of $12^\circ$.
B The third and higher orders are not produced.
C A grating with more lines per metre could produce more orders.
D Total number of maximas produced is 7.

stemImage.alt: Question 19: Monochromatic light of wavelength 490 nm falls normally on a diffraction grating that has 6 x 105 lines per metre. Which one of the following is correct?

appearances.originalFile: TJC/H2 Physics/2026 H2 Prelim Paper 1 final.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must convert line density to spacing, bound the order and count both sides.
questions.misconception: The highest order equals the number of maxima.

explanation.body: Use $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$, with $d=1/(6\times10^5)\ \mathrm{m}$. For $n=1$, $\sin\theta=(490\times10^{-9})/d$ gives $\theta=17^\circ$. Since $\sin\theta\leq1$, $n\leq d/\lambda=3.4$, so the highest order is 3. There are $2(3)+1=7$ maxima including the central maximum.

perOption.A: The grating equation gives a first-order angle of $17^\circ$.
perOption.B: The third order is still allowed because $3\lambda/d<1$.
perOption.C: Increasing the line density decreases the spacing and lowers the upper bound on the order.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.stemText:
$S_1$ and $S_2$ are two wave generators producing waves of intensity $0.36I$ and $0.25I$ respectively at P. A resultant intensity minima occurs at P as shown in the diagram below.

[Diagram: two sources $S_1$ (upper) and $S_2$ (lower) on the left, with straight lines drawn from each to a point P at the upper right.]

What is the resultant intensity at point P in terms of $I$?

A  zero
B  $0.010I$
C  $0.11I$
D  $0.31I$

stemImage.alt: Question 12: S1 and S2 are two wave generators producing waves of intensity 0.36I and 0.25I respectively at P. A resultant intensity minima occurs at P as shown in the diagr

appearances.originalFile: grail:15121 TMJC_2024_H2 Physics P1_QP_AS

questions.difficultyReason: Needs the intensity–amplitude relation and the realisation that amplitudes, not intensities, subtract at a minimum.
questions.misconception: Subtracting intensities instead of amplitudes

explanation.body:
Since $I \propto A^2$: $\dfrac{I_1}{I_2} = \dfrac{A_1^2}{A_2^2} \Rightarrow \sqrt{\dfrac{0.36}{0.25}} = \dfrac{A_1}{A_2} \Rightarrow A_1 = 1.2A_2$.

At P (a minimum) the waves arrive in antiphase, so the resultant amplitude is $A_P = 1.2A_2 - A_2 = 0.2A_2$.

$\dfrac{I_P}{0.25I} = \dfrac{(0.2A_2)^2}{A_2^2} = 0.040 \Rightarrow I_P = 0.010I$.

Equivalently, $A_P = 0.6A - 0.5A = 0.1A$, so $I_P = 0.010I$.

perOption.A: Zero only if the two waves had equal amplitudes; here the amplitudes differ.
perOption.B: Correct. Amplitudes subtract: $(0.6-0.5)^2 I = 0.010I$.
perOption.C: Subtracts the intensities ($0.36I - 0.25I$) instead of the amplitudes.
perOption.D: Does not come from subtracting amplitudes and squaring; intensities cannot be combined linearly.

explanation.body:
Points in alternate segments (loops) of a standing wave are in antiphase, with a phase difference of $\pi$, while points in the same segment, or in segments two apart, are in phase.

X is in the first segment, so the point in the adjacent (second) segment, B, has a phase difference of $\pi$ with X.

perOption.B: Correct. B is in the adjacent segment, so it is in antiphase with X.
perOption.C: C is two segments away from X, so it is in phase with X.
perOption.D: D is two segments away from X, so it is in phase with X.

questions.stemText:
A wire is stretched between two supports and plucked. A stationary wave is formed as shown.

[Diagram: a wire between two fixed supports vibrating in a single loop, with nodes at both supports and an antinode in the middle (solid and dashed curves show the extreme positions).]

Given that the frequency of the stationary wave shown above is $f$, what is the next possible frequency for a stationary wave to be formed in the setup?

A $2f$
B $3f$
C $\frac{1}{2}f$
D $\frac{3}{2}f$

stemImage.alt: Question 12: A wire is stretched between two supports and plucked. A stationary wave is formed as shown. Given that the frequency of the stationary wave shown above is f, wh

appearances.originalFile: grail:19911 TMJC_2025_H2 Physics_P1_QP

questions.difficultyReason: Standard harmonic reasoning for a string fixed at both ends, read off a simple diagram.
questions.misconception: Thinking only odd harmonics are allowed on a string fixed at both ends

explanation.body:
The two supports must be nodes. Taking the distance between the supports as $L$, the wave shown (one loop) has wavelength $2L$, and the next possible stationary wave (two loops) has wavelength $L$.

Using $v = f\lambda$ with the same wave speed: $f = \dfrac{v}{2L}$ and $f' = \dfrac{v}{L} = 2f$.

perOption.A: Correct. The next mode has two loops, halving the wavelength and doubling the frequency.
perOption.B: $3f$ is the third harmonic; it skips the two-loop mode, as if only odd harmonics were allowed (as in a pipe closed at one end).
perOption.C: $\tfrac{1}{2}f$ would need wavelength $4L$, which cannot have nodes at both supports; the mode shown is already the lowest.
perOption.D: $\tfrac{3}{2}f$ would need 1.5 loops, leaving an antinode at a fixed support.

questions.stemText:
Two monochromatic radiations X and Y of wavelengths $\lambda_X$ and $\lambda_Y$ respectively, are incident normally on a diffraction grating. The third order intensity maximum for X coincides with the fifth order intensity maximum for Y.

What is the ratio of $\dfrac{\lambda_X}{\lambda_Y}$?

A $\frac{1}{2}$
B $\frac{3}{5}$
C $\frac{5}{3}$
D Not able to determine with given information.

questions.difficultyReason: One-line ratio from the grating equation; main risk is inverting the ratio.
questions.misconception: Inverting the ratio (higher order means shorter wavelength)

explanation.body:
For a diffraction grating, $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$. Coinciding maxima are at the same angle $\theta$ for the same grating spacing $d$, so

$3\lambda_X = 5\lambda_Y$

$\dfrac{\lambda_X}{\lambda_Y} = \dfrac{5}{3}$

perOption.A: Has no basis in the orders given; the ratio follows from $3\lambda_X = 5\lambda_Y$.
perOption.B: Inverts the ratio: $3/5$ is $\lambda_Y/\lambda_X$.
perOption.C: Correct. $3\lambda_X = 5\lambda_Y$ gives $\lambda_X/\lambda_Y = 5/3$.
perOption.D: $d$ and $\sin\theta$ are the same for both, so they cancel and the ratio can be found.

questions.stem:
Two waves of equal frequency and amplitude are travelling in opposite directions along a stretched string. When they meet, they form a stationary wave with three nodes and two antinodes. The frequency of both waves is doubled and a new stationary wave is formed.

How many antinodes are there in the new stationary wave?
questions.stemText: Two waves of equal frequency and amplitude are travelling in opposite directions along a stretched string. When they meet, they form a stationary wave with three nodes and two antinodes. The frequency of both waves is doubled and a new stationary wave is formed. How many antinodes are there in the new stationary wave? A 1 B 3 C 4 D 5

appearances.originalFile: grail:19928 VJC 2025 J2 H2 Phy Prelim Paper 1

questions.difficultyReason: Simple reasoning about loops per wavelength when frequency doubles.
questions.misconception: Confusing nodes with antinodes

explanation.body:
A stationary wave with three nodes and two antinodes is two loops long, so the length is one wavelength.

When the frequency is doubled, the wavelength is halved, so the same length now holds two wavelengths, i.e. four loops.

Hence there are 4 antinodes.

perOption.A: Fewer antinodes would require a longer wavelength, i.e. a lower frequency.
perOption.B: Adds one antinode instead of doubling the number of loops.
perOption.C: Correct. Halving $\lambda$ doubles the number of loops from 2 to 4.
perOption.D: Counts nodes (5) instead of antinodes.

questions.difficultyReason: Requires knowing that displacement nodes are pressure antinodes for sound.

explanation.body:
At a displacement node the air particles do not move, so displacement is minimum (zero).

The particles on either side move towards it, then away from it, together. The air there is alternately compressed and rarefied, so the pressure change is maximum.

perOption.D: A node by definition has minimum displacement.

questions.stemText: In a single-slit diffraction experiment, a laser with a wavelength of 600 nm is aimed at a slit of width 0.20 mm and the resulting diffraction pattern is observed on a screen 2.0 m away. What is the width of the central maximum of the diffraction pattern? A 0.0030 mm B 0.0060 mm C 6.0 mm D 12 mm

appearances.originalFile: grail:10487 YIJC 2023 H2Phy Prelim P1 Question Paper

questions.difficultyReason: Needs the first-minimum condition plus the doubling for the full central width.
questions.misconception: Taking the half-width as the full width of the central maximum

explanation.body:
For single-slit diffraction, the first minimum is at $\sin\theta = \dfrac{\lambda}{b} = \dfrac{600\times10^{-9}}{0.20\times10^{-3}}$, so $\theta = 0.0030\ \mathrm{rad}$.

Distance from centre to first minimum: $s = r\theta = 2.0\times0.0030 = 0.0060\ \mathrm{m}$.

Width of central maximum $\approx 2s = 2\times0.0060 = 0.012\ \mathrm{m} = 12\ \mathrm{mm}$.

perOption.A: This is the angle $\theta$ in radians (0.0030), not a width on the screen.
perOption.B: Misreads $s = 0.0060\ \mathrm{m}$ as millimetres.
perOption.C: This is $s$, the half-width; the central maximum spans from one first minimum to the other.
perOption.D: Correct. Width $= 2D\lambda/b$.

The speed of sound in air is 330 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The frequency of the sound from the loudspeaker is now increased to the next higher resonance of air in the tube. What is the new frequency of the sound?

The speed of sound in air is 330 m s−1. The frequency of the sound from the loudspeaker is now increased to the next higher resonance of air in the tube. What is the new frequency of the sound? A 138 Hz B 413 Hz C 688 Hz D 963 Hz

appearances.originalFile: grail:14610 YIJC 2024 JC2 PRELIM H2 Phy P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Must identify the current mode from the diagram and know only odd harmonics exist in a closed tube.
questions.misconception: Thinking the next resonance adds a half wavelength rather than stepping to the next odd quarter

explanation.body:
The tube is closed at the bottom (node) and open at the top (antinode). The current pattern is $\frac{3}{4}\lambda$; the next higher resonance is $\frac{5}{4}\lambda$.

$\frac{5}{4}\lambda = 60\ \mathrm{cm} \Rightarrow \lambda = 48\ \mathrm{cm} = 0.48\ \mathrm{m}$

$v = f\lambda$: $330 = f(0.48)$, so $f = 688\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

perOption.A: Fundamental ($\frac{1}{4}\lambda = 60$ cm), a lower resonance not a higher one.
perOption.B: The current resonance ($\frac{3}{4}\lambda = 60$ cm), not the next higher one.
perOption.C: Correct. $\frac{5}{4}\lambda = 0.60$ m gives 688 Hz.
perOption.D: Skips a harmonic ($\frac{7}{4}\lambda = 60$ cm).

The intensity of the wave from S1 is 4I while the intensity of the wave from S2 is I. The waves meet at point P to form a bright fringe due to constructive interference and meet at point Q to form a dark fringe due to destructive interference. What is the ratio of the intensity of light at point P to the intensity of light at point Q? A 0.11 B 1.7 C 4.0 D 9.0

appearances.originalFile: YIJC/2026 JC2 H2 Prelim Paper 1 QP (Revised).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires converting intensities to amplitudes before combining and squaring them.
questions.misconception: Adding or subtracting intensities directly.

explanation.body: Since $I=kA^2$, if the amplitude from $S_2$ is $A$, the amplitude from $S_1$ is $2A$. The resultant amplitude is $2A+A=3A$ at P and $2A-A=A$ at Q. Thus $\frac{I_P}{I_Q}=\frac{(3A)^2}{A^2}=9.0$.

perOption.A: Reverses the bright-to-dark intensity ratio.
perOption.B: Adds and subtracts intensities directly, giving $5/3$.
perOption.C: Uses the source intensity ratio without combining the waves.
perOption.D: Correct.

What is the total number of bright spots that are produced?
questions.stemText: Light of wavelength 690 nm passes through a diffraction grating with 300 lines per mm, producing a series of bright spots (maxima) on a screen. What is the total number of bright spots that are produced? A 4 B 8 C 9 D 11

appearances.originalFile: YIJC/2026 JC2 H2 Prelim Paper 1 QP (Revised).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires converting line density to spacing, finding the highest integer order and counting both sides.
questions.misconception: Omitting the zero-order maximum.

explanation.body: Use $a\sin\theta=n\lambda$. At $\theta=90^\circ$, $\frac{1}{300\times1000}\sin90^\circ=n(690\times10^{-9})$, giving an order limit of about $4.83$. The highest observable integer order is $4$, so there are $4+1+4=9$ bright spots.

perOption.A: Counts the nonzero orders on only one side.
perOption.B: Omits the central maximum.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Rounds the order limit up to five even though the fifth order would require $\sin\theta>1$.
